name: Iris Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, that's fine. I've done surveys before but never a proper chat like this.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Great. Could you walk me through a normal working day, start to finish?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work days at a fashion warehouse for an online clothes shop, on the edge of town by the old brickworks. Half my week is picking, the other half is returns, which is opening bags of stuff people sent back, checking for make-up stains and tags, and deciding if it goes back on the shelf or to the outlet. Seven till half three, and I walk about twenty thousand steps. Returns is the bit I'm actually good at, you get a feel for whether a dress has been worn to a wedding.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The targets in peak, from October to January, when it's compulsory overtime and the agency people come in and don't know anything. And the pay, honestly, I'm on £11.60 and my partner Theo drives buses, so between us we cover rent and that's about it. I've got maybe three weeks of money if something went wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the hype was overblown, but it doesn't mean everything's fine for warehouse workers. I'd post something about pay, because that's the real story. Nobody was going to give us a rise because of AI anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the same squeeze. The returns software already uses some AI to sort the easy ones, so maybe it does a bit more of that and I spend more time picking. Rent went up £60 in the spring, and the shop is cutting the free returns, which means fewer returns jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and push the union to get a recognition vote, because right now we haven't even got one at our site. I'd try to get on the returns quality team permanently, it's 40p more an hour. And I'd keep using the AI chat thing now and then for writing my union emails, it helps with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired more than worried. It's the same fight we've already got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fewer returns jobs. How many people are on returns now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About twenty on days. Last year it was twenty-six, they just didn't replace people who left. Nobody announced anything at the returns bench, there were just fewer coats on the pegs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a recognition vote change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the union can actually bargain over pay and the targets, instead of just helping people one by one at disciplinaries. Me and Kerry from returns have been signing people up at the bus stop. We're at about 35 percent.

say: I'd say the **hype** was overblown, but warehouse work still isn't fine.
I'd post about **pay**, because that's the real story for us.
think: It's the **same squeeze**: rent went up £60 and returns work is shrinking.
Returns went from **26 to 20** people without anyone announcing it.
do: Push for a **union recognition** vote at her site, signing people up at the bus stop.
Try for the permanent **returns quality** team, which pays 40p an hour more.
Keep using an **AI chat tool** now and then to draft union emails.
feel: More **tired** than worried, because it's the same fight she already has.
S0.quote: Nobody announced anything at the returns bench, there were just fewer coats on the pegs.
fieldNote: Pressure here comes from **rent** and shrinking returns, not from AI itself.
She's quietly **organising**: signing people up at the bus stop with a colleague.
Uses **AI** for union emails, a practical not a fearful relationship with it.

steps.text: Sign up colleagues at the bus stop for a union recognition vote
Apply for the permanent returns quality team at 40p more
Use an AI chat tool to draft union letters and emails

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance to get decent rules in place before the robots arrive, not after. Online I'd share stuff about the four-day week and about firms paying their share. At work I'd say this is why we need the union, now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means the returns bench gets cut first, because deciding if a dress is resellable is basically a photo and a decision. A camera and AI could do most of that. Picking stays a person for a few more years, so I'd probably get pushed back to picking full time, which is harder on my knees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the union push, that's my first year. I'd look at the forklift and reach-truck licence, the company does it for free if you sign for a year. I'd sit down with Theo and set up a £40 a month standing order, small but something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I think. I can see the bit of the job I'm good at going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of returns do you think goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sorting of the easy ones, unworn, tags on, that's already partly automatic. Then the stain check, once a camera can spot foundation on a collar. What's left is the weird stuff, a wedding dress with a note in the pocket, and that's one person not twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you worried about anyone in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kerry, because she's 54 and she's only ever done returns. I'd be all right picking for a while. Kerry's knees are worse than mine.

say: I'd say it's a chance to get **decent rules** in place before the robots, not after.
I'd share posts about a **four-day week** and firms paying their share.
think: The **returns bench** goes first, because judging a dress is a photo and a decision.
I'd get pushed back to **full-time picking**, which is harder on my knees.
do: Finish the **union recognition** push in the first year.
Sign up for the free **reach-truck licence** in return for a year's tie-in.
Set up a **£40 a month** standing order with her partner.
feel: **Anxious**, because she can see the part of the job she's good at going.
S1.quote: Deciding if a dress is resellable is basically a photo and a decision. A camera and AI could do most of that.
fieldNote: She knows exactly which tasks go first, down to **foundation on a collar**.
Her answer mixes **organising** with a personal backup: the reach-truck licence.
Worries more for **Kerry**, an older colleague, than for herself.

steps.text: Win the union recognition vote at the fashion warehouse
Take the company's free reach-truck licence with a one-year tie-in
Set up a £40 a month standing order with Theo

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a basic income, a proper one, and I'd say it loudly. I'd go to the protests. At work I'd say the people who made the money from us should be paying for what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the online shop's office goes in 2028, the buyers and the customer service, and they're the ones who make the targets. The returns bench goes with that. Then about 2031 robots can pick and pack, and I've got nothing to fall back on but a reach-truck licence that a robot doesn't need either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look properly at jobs the robots get to last. I've thought about bus driving like Theo, but self-driving buses might come first, so maybe a nursing assistant course at the college. I'd save every overtime shift, maybe £150 a month in peak. And I'd be on the union committee for the redundancy talks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like when the lights flicker in the warehouse and you don't know if they'll come back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three years between AGI and the robots change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the only good bit. Three years is enough for a healthcare course if I start straight away, part time around shifts. If I wait for the robots to show up in the aisles, it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Theo change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We were going to try for a baby in a couple of years. We'd probably wait, and that's a horrible thing to say out loud. You can't have a baby on a reach-truck licence and three weeks of savings.

say: I'd say it's the moment for a proper **basic income**, and go to protests.
I'd say the people who **profited** from us should pay for what comes next.
think: The shop's **office** goes in 2028, and the returns bench goes with it.
By **2031** robots pick and pack, and a reach-truck licence won't save me.
do: Start a part-time **healthcare course** at the college straight away.
Save every **overtime shift** in peak, about £150 a month.
Join the **union committee** for redundancy talks.
feel: **Alarmed**, like the warehouse lights flickering and not knowing if they'll come back.
S2.quote: You can't have a baby on a reach-truck licence and three weeks of savings.
fieldNote: She uses the **three-year gap** as a window to start a healthcare course now.
Would **postpone a baby** with her partner; said it was horrible to say out loud.
Still puts **collective action** first, alongside her personal plan.

steps.text: Enrol on a part-time nursing assistant course at the college
Bank every peak overtime shift, about £150 a month
Sit on the union committee for redundancy talks
Put off trying for a baby with Theo

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but I'd say five years is enough to do it properly, so no excuses. Retraining paid for by the companies, a levy on robots. I'd be pushing that in the union and at the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking side, eight for the robots, so I'd be 35 when picking goes. That's a lot of time to get out and into something else. I still think it's grim for the people who don't move, but for me it's manageable if I start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the reach-truck licence in year one, because it still pays a bit more in the meantime. Then the healthcare course in year two, evenings. Keep the £40 a month going and push it to £60 when Theo gets his pay rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but less, there's a path. I'd still lose sleep in peak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said manageable. But the job still goes. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. The job goes, that's not changing. Manageable means I'd have a different job lined up when it does, if I'm not lazy about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from your employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time off for the course without losing my shift pattern. That's it really. Shift swaps are the thing that kills people's courses, not the fees.

say: I'd say five years is enough to do **retraining** properly, so no excuses.
I'd push a **levy on robots** in the union and at the council.
think: I'd be **35** when picking goes, enough time to get into something else.
It's **grim** for people who don't move, but manageable for me if I start.
do: Get the **reach-truck licence** in year one for the extra pay meanwhile.
Start an evening **healthcare course** in year two.
Raise savings from **£40 to £60** a month when her partner's rise comes.
feel: **Anxious but less**, because there's a path, though peak still costs her sleep.
S3.quote: Shift swaps are the thing that kills people's courses, not the fees.
fieldNote: Holds two truths: the **job goes**, but she'd have something lined up.
Her practical ask is **shift stability** for study, not money.
She sequences it: licence first, then **healthcare** course.

steps.text: Get the reach-truck licence in the first year
Start an evening healthcare course in year two
Raise the standing order from £40 to £60 a month
Press the council for a retraining levy on robot firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is our chance to get it right. Pay, training, shorter weeks. I'd share that everywhere, it's the hopeful version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years for AGI and about thirteen for the robots, so 2039, I'd be 40. I'd have time to do healthcare properly, maybe even a nursing degree part time. The thing that still bothers me is that with three weeks of savings, one bad month knocks any plan over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd do the reach-truck licence and stay on the union push. I'd start a small emergency pot, aim for £1,000 by the end of the year. Then look at the healthcare apprenticeship in a couple of years once it's proven people get jobs from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, honestly, because of money, not the robots. The robots feel far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one bad month you're thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Theo's bus depot changing his shifts, or my knees going. Either one and we're on the credit card. We had that two years ago with his hernia and it took a year to pay off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new starter at the warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the licence, join the union, and don't think of the job as forever. I'd say it nicely. They're usually nineteen and think they'll be gone in six months, and then it's eight years.

say: I'd say **ten years** is our chance to get pay, training and shorter weeks right.
I'd share it everywhere as the **hopeful** version.
think: With robots around **2039** I'd have time for healthcare or a nursing degree.
With **three weeks** of savings, one bad month knocks any plan over.
do: Get the **reach-truck licence** and keep the union push going.
Build a **£1,000** emergency pot by the end of the first year.
Look at a **healthcare apprenticeship** once it's proven to lead to jobs.
feel: Still **anxious**, about money more than robots, which feel far away.
S4.quote: With three weeks of savings, one bad month knocks any plan over.
fieldNote: The decade calms the **robot** worry but not the **money** worry.
A partner's **hernia** two years ago took a year to pay off on the credit card.
She waits for proof, wanting the **apprenticeship** shown to work before signing.

steps.text: Get the reach-truck licence in the first year
Build a £1,000 emergency pot by year end
Keep signing colleagues up for the union
Wait for proof the healthcare apprenticeship leads to jobs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because of the baby thing more than the job. What would help is a guaranteed income while you retrain, and childcare, so people like me and Theo don't have to choose between a family and a course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how the targets feel. Everyone thinks the robot is the scary thing, but the wrist scanner beeping at you is already a bit of a robot boss. We're halfway there.

headlineQuote: Everyone thinks the robot is the scary thing, but the wrist scanner beeping at you is already a bit of a robot boss.
portrait: **Iris** is 27, picks and handles **returns** at an online fashion warehouse, and lives with her partner, a bus driver.
She has about **three weeks** of savings and rent that rose £60 this year.
She leans left and is **organising** a union recognition vote, while quietly planning a personal backup.
She moves once things are proven: **reach-truck licence** first, then a healthcare course.
Her moods run uneasy to **alarmed**, with AGI by 2028 making her put off a baby.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, mostly because she'd postpone having a **baby** with her partner.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed income** while retraining, plus **childcare** so family and study aren't a choice.
